Simulate a study with partial verification

Source: R/simulate.R
simulate_study.Rd

Generates individual data for a study in which K binary tests are applied to all subjects, but only some of them are verified by the reference standard. For each subject the disease status is drawn first, then the K test results and finally the verification, which depends on the response profile (the vector of test results) and, when odds_ratio is not 1, also on the disease status. Useful for examples, tests and simulation studies.

Usage

simulate_study(
  n,
  prevalence,
  sensitivity,
  specificity,
  verification_prob,
  odds_ratio = 1,
  dependence = independence()
)

Arguments

n

Number of subjects: a single whole number, at least 1. No default.

prevalence

Probability of disease: a single number in \([0, 1]\). No default.

sensitivity

Sensitivity of each test: a numeric vector with values in \([0, 1]\), one element per test, of length K >= 1. No default. The names of sensitivity, if present, become the names of the test columns of the output; if it has no names, the tests are called T1, ..., TK. The names verified and disease are not allowed.

specificity

Specificity of each test: a numeric vector with values in \([0, 1]\) and the same length as sensitivity; its k-th element is the specificity of the k-th test. Its names are ignored. No default.

verification_prob

Probability of verification of healthy subjects, with values in \([0, 1]\). It is either a single number, which applies to all response profiles, or a vector of length \(2^K\) with one number per response profile, in binary order: the profile \(t\) is at position \(1 + \sum_k t_k 2^{k-1}\), so the first profile is the one with all tests negative and the first test changes fastest. With K = 2 the order is (0,0), (1,0), (0,1), (1,1). A value 0 means that the profile is never verified and a value 1 that it is always verified. No default.

odds_ratio

Odds ratio of verification between diseased and healthy subjects with the same response profile: a single positive number, the same for all profiles. Default 1, which gives verification that is missing at random (it does not depend on the disease status). Values greater than 1 make diseased subjects more likely to be verified, values between 0 and 1 less likely; any value different from 1 gives verification that is missing not at random.

dependence

How the test results depend on each other given the disease status: a single dependence mechanism, one of dependence = independence() (the tests are independent given the disease status), dependence = latent_dependence(...) (the tests share a normal latent variable, with one loading per test and disease class) or dependence = probit_dependence(...) (the tests have jointly normal latent variables, with one correlation per pair of tests and disease class). Default independence(). Whatever the mechanism, sensitivity and specificity remain the marginal sensitivity and specificity of each test.

Value

A data frame with one row per subject and the following columns: one 0/1 column for each test, always observed, named as described in sensitivity; verified (0/1); disease (0/1 for verified subjects, NA for unverified subjects).

Details

For each subject the function simulates:

  • the disease status \(D\), Bernoulli with probability prevalence;

  • the K test results \(T_1, \dots, T_K\) given \(D\), with \(P(T_k = 1 \mid D = 1)\) equal to sensitivity[k] and \(P(T_k = 0 \mid D = 0)\) equal to specificity[k]. The tests are independent given \(D\) with dependence = independence(), and dependent given \(D\) with the other values of dependence (see the paragraph on the dependence between tests below);

  • the verification \(V\), Bernoulli with probability \(\lambda_{t,d} = P(V = 1 \mid T = t, D = d)\).

The verification probability of a healthy subject with profile \(t\) is \(\lambda_{t,0}\) = verification_prob for that profile. The verification probability of a diseased subject with the same profile is \(\lambda_{t,1} = \mathrm{expit}(\mathrm{logit}\,\lambda_{t,0} + \log(\mathrm{odds\_ratio}))\), so that the odds of verification of diseased subjects are odds_ratio times the odds for healthy subjects with the same profile (Kosinski and Barnhart, 2003).

Dependence between the tests. The argument dependence sets the joint distribution of the K results within each disease class, that is the probabilities \(\theta_{d,t} = P(T = t \mid D = d)\) of the response profiles \(t\) among the diseased (\(d = 1\)) and among the healthy (\(d = 0\)). Every mechanism keeps the sensitivities and specificities given in sensitivity and specificity as the marginal probabilities, and changes only how often the tests are right or wrong together (Vacek, 1985; Torrance-Rynard and Walter, 1997):

  • dependence = independence(): \(\theta_{1,t} = \prod_k Se_k^{t_k}(1 - Se_k)^{1 - t_k}\) and \(\theta_{0,t} = \prod_k (1 - Sp_k)^{t_k} Sp_k^{1 - t_k}\);

  • dependence = latent_dependence(diseased_loadings, healthy_loadings): each subject has a latent variable \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\) (Qu et al., 1996; Dendukuri and Joseph, 2001), independent of \(D\), and given \(D = d\) and \(Z = z\) the tests are independent with \(P(T_k = 1 \mid D = d, Z = z) = \Phi(a_{dk} + b_{dk} z)\), where \(b_{dk}\) is the loading of test \(k\) in class \(d\) and \(a_{dk}\) is chosen so that the marginal probabilities are the sensitivities and specificities. Tests \(j\) and \(k\) are positively dependent when \(b_{dj} b_{dk} > 0\) and negatively dependent when \(b_{dj} b_{dk} < 0\);

  • dependence = probit_dependence(diseased_correlation, healthy_correlation): given \(D = d\), test \(k\) is positive when a standard normal latent variable \(Y_k\) falls below a threshold that gives the required sensitivity or specificity, and the latent variables of the K tests are jointly normal with correlation matrix \(R_d\) (Qu et al., 1996; Dendukuri and Joseph, 2001). The element \(R_{d,jk}\) is the correlation, of any sign, between tests \(j\) and \(k\) in class \(d\).

The size of the loadings or of the correlation matrices is checked here against the number of tests K, which the dependence mechanism does not know when it is created. A correlation matrix that is not positive definite for K tests gives an error.

Supported data-generating mechanisms.

  • any number K >= 1 of tests, with arbitrary prevalence, sensitivities and specificities, with tests that are independent given the disease status or dependent through one of the mechanisms above;

  • verification that depends on the response profile only, with the same probability for all profiles (a single verification_prob) or with one probability per profile. A value 0 means that the profile is never verified, a value 1 that it is always verified (for healthy subjects; see odds_ratio for diseased subjects);

  • missing at random verification (odds_ratio = 1), where verification depends only on the profile (Rubin, 1976), and missing not at random verification (odds_ratio different from 1), where the odds of verification also depend on the disease status through the same odds ratio for all profiles (Kosinski and Barnhart, 2003). Profiles with verification probability 0 or 1 are never verified, or always verified, whatever odds_ratio is.

Not supported: dependence between the tests given the disease status other than through the two latent mechanisms above (for example log-linear interactions given as odds ratios), covariates, verification that depends on something other than the response profile and the disease status, and a disease-dependent verification whose odds ratio differs across profiles.

References

Dendukuri, N. and Joseph, L. (2001). Bayesian approaches to modeling the conditional dependence between multiple diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 57(1), 158–167. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2001.00158.x

Kosinski, A. S. and Barnhart, H. X. (2003). Accounting for nonignorable verification bias in assessment of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 59(1), 163–171. doi:10.1111/1541-0420.00019

Qu, Y., Tan, M. and Kutner, M. H. (1996). Random effects models in latent class analysis for evaluating accuracy of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 52(3), 797–810. doi:10.2307/2533043

Rubin, D. B. (1976). Inference and missing data. Biometrika, 63(3), 581–592. doi:10.1093/biomet/63.3.581

Torrance-Rynard, V. L. and Walter, S. D. (1997). Effects of dependent errors in the assessment of diagnostic test performance. Statistics in Medicine, 16(19), 2157–2175. doi:10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19971015)16:19<2157::AID-SIM653>3.0.CO;2-X

Vacek, P. M. (1985). The effect of conditional dependence on the evaluation of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 41(4), 959–968. doi:10.2307/2530967

See also

independence(), latent_dependence(), probit_dependence()

Examples

set.seed(1)

# Two tests, verification depending only on the results (MAR): subjects
# negative to both tests are verified with probability 0.1, the others with
# probability 0.9 or 1. The profiles are in the order (0,0), (1,0), (0,1), (1,1).
d <- simulate_study(n = 500, prevalence = 0.2,
                    sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.7),
                    specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.95),
                    verification_prob = c(0.1, 0.9, 0.9, 1))
head(d)
#>   A B verified disease
#> 1 0 0        0      NA
#> 2 0 0        0      NA
#> 3 0 0        0      NA
#> 4 1 0        1       1
#> 5 0 0        0      NA
#> 6 0 1        1       1
# proportion of verified subjects by profile
tapply(d$verified, paste(d$A, d$B), mean)
#>       0 0       0 1       1 0       1 1 
#> 0.1057402 0.8333333 0.9078947 1.0000000 

# Everyone verified: a single verification probability equal to 1
d_full <- simulate_study(n = 500, prevalence = 0.2,
                         sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.7),
                         specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.95),
                         verification_prob = 1)
mean(d_full$verified)
#> [1] 1

# A never-verified profile: only subjects positive to at least one test are
# verified, so the disease status is missing for every (0,0) subject
d_screen <- simulate_study(n = 500, prevalence = 0.2,
                           sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.7),
                           specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.95),
                           verification_prob = c(0, 1, 1, 1))
table(paste(d_screen$A, d_screen$B), d_screen$verified)
#>      
#>         0   1
#>   0 0 305   0
#>   0 1   0  23
#>   1 0   0  99
#>   1 1   0  73

# Verification that depends on the disease (MNAR): with odds_ratio = 3 the
# odds of verification are three times higher for the diseased, so among
# the verified the diseased are over-represented
d_mnar <- simulate_study(n = 5000, prevalence = 0.2,
                         sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.7),
                         specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.95),
                         verification_prob = 0.3, odds_ratio = 3)
mean(d_mnar$disease, na.rm = TRUE)   # well above the prevalence 0.2
#> [1] 0.3348066

# Three tests without names: the columns are called T1, T2, T3, and there
# are 2^3 = 8 profiles, so verification_prob has 8 values
d3 <- simulate_study(n = 500, prevalence = 0.1,
                     sensitivity = c(0.9, 0.8, 0.7),
                     specificity = c(0.9, 0.9, 0.95),
                     verification_prob = c(0.05, rep(0.8, 6), 1))
names(d3)
#> [1] "T1"       "T2"       "T3"       "verified" "disease" 

# Three tests dependent given the disease: among the diseased tests A and B
# share a latent severity, C much less; among the healthy only A and B
# are (weakly) dependent
d_dep <- simulate_study(n = 5000, prevalence = 0.2,
                        sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.8, C = 0.7),
                        specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.9, C = 0.95),
                        verification_prob = c(0.05, rep(0.8, 6), 1),
                        dependence = latent_dependence(
                          diseased_loadings = c(1, 1, 0.3),
                          healthy_loadings = c(0.5, 0.5, 0)))
sick <- which(d_dep$disease == 1)
cor(d_dep[sick, c("A", "B", "C")])
#>            A          B          C
#> A 1.00000000 0.10113242 0.02708195
#> B 0.10113242 1.00000000 0.07264363
#> C 0.02708195 0.07264363 1.00000000

# Correlation 0.4 between every pair of tests among the diseased and -0.2
# among the healthy
d_probit <- simulate_study(n = 5000, prevalence = 0.2,
                           sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.8, C = 0.7),
                           specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.9, C = 0.95),
                           verification_prob = 1,
                           dependence = probit_dependence(
                             diseased_correlation = 0.4,
                             healthy_correlation = -0.2))
